title: Serological, Molecular and Clinicopathological Evidence of Malignant Catarrhal Fever in Buffaloes (Bubalus bubalis) from Western Maharashtra, India
content: Malignant catarrhal fever (MCF) is a viral disease in which sheep act as asymptomatic reservoirs of ovine gammaherpesvirus-2 (OvHV-2), while cattle and buffaloes may develop severe, often fatal disease. Despite India’s large buffalo population, studies on buffalo MCF have largely been limited to PCR-based prevalence surveys. This study investigated a cohort of buffaloes from five districts of Western Maharashtra using serological and molecular assays, together with necropsy and histopathological examination of a fatal case. Among 180 buffalo sera tested by MCF-antibody ELISA, 15 (8.33%; 95% CI: 5.1–13.3%) were seropositive, distributed across eight of 24 farms (33.33%; 95% CI: 18.0–53.3%). Heminested PCR targeting the OvHV-2 tegument protein gene (ORF75, encoding FGARAT) detected viral DNA in seven of 200 blood samples (3.5%; 95% CI: 1.7–7.0%). Nested PCR targeting the polymerase gene of alcelaphine gammaherpesvirus-1 (AlHV-1) did not detect viral DNA in any sample. However, the absence of a positive control limits the interpretation of these negative findings. Two of 200 buffaloes (1%) developed clinical signs consistent with MCF and subsequently died. One case was confirmed by necropsy and histopathological examination, while the second was considered presumptive based on characteristic clinical signs and PCR-positive blood. Necropsy revealed hepatomegaly with multifocal necrosis, hemorrhagic and necrotic lymphadenitis, epicardial hemorrhage, and splenic congestion. Histopathological examination demonstrated vasculitis, lymphocytic infiltration, and multifocal organ necrosis. OvHV-2 infection in the necropsied animal was confirmed by heminested PCR of lymph node and spleen tissues and by antemortem ELISA. These findings provide an integrated serological, molecular, clinical, and pathological characterization of MCF in buffaloes from Western Maharashtra, identifying OvHV-2 as the principal etiological agent detected in the study and highlighting the need for further epidemiological and differential diagnostic investigations.
